clue.text: Like The Lark, put ad around shelter

indicators.note: letters moved around are no longer in their printed order, so the two short words are rearranged

parts.note: two short words used as letters to rearrange
as a verb, to shelter under an awning, a sense the setter takes from the same root

explanation.surface: An advert for something lark-like is being placed around a shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lark Ascending, by Vaughan Williams, regularly tops the Classic FM Hall of Fame; the lark is the early riser of proverb. AWN as 'shelter' is a stretch, from awning.
explanation.definitionFit: Larks are proverbially early risers, and an early bird is out of bed when the sun first comes up.

clue.text: Brahms and Liszt used to put people out

explanation.walkthrough: The composers are not music at all: in Cockney rhyming slang Brahms and Liszt means pissed, a British word for drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone ousted has been removed or expelled from a position, which is what putting people out of it does.

clue.text: What's produced at three regularly? Yes!

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition as well as the wordplay. Three o'clock is the traditional British hour for afternoon tea.
explanation.definitionFit: Afternoon tea is carried in on a flat board with cups and pot, so that board is what gets brought out mid-afternoon.

explanation.definitionFit: A clerihew is a short humorous rhyming poem about a famous person, so Bentley teased in verse is one.

explanation.definitionFit: Etnean means relating to Mount Etna, a fiery volcano in Sicily, which is the European mountain with a hot head.
